title: Debates on the BBC and the next autism strategy
label: 17 November 2026 · BBC and autism debates
summary: The committee heard requests for debates on the BBC’s future and the Government’s next national autism strategy. Grahame Morris argued that MPs should question Ministers about BBC cuts and the broadcaster’s future before Christmas, preferring a debate in the main Commons chamber but accepting Westminster Hall if necessary. Alison Hume set out serious inequalities faced by autistic people and asked for a timely debate while the new strategy is being developed.

A debate in a separate House of Commons debating room, rather than the main chamber.
A law requiring the Government to publish and regularly update a strategy for supporting autistic people.

chapters.title: The BBC’s future
chapters.takeaway: Grahame Morris wants MPs to question Ministers about BBC cuts before the next charter takes effect, ideally in a chamber debate before Christmas.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: First, Grahame Morris is asking for a debate about the future of the BBC. He hopes it can happen before Christmas, when the Government is expected to publish a plan for the broadcaster.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: This debate isn’t about the future of this committee; it’s about the BBC. The BBC is already making decisions about jobs and programmes, including cuts affecting BBC Scotland and news channels. Those choices will shape the service under its next BBC charter.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: MPs should have the chance to put their constituents’ views on record and ask Ministers how they’ll respond. In my area, BBC Radio Newcastle and Look North show why local radio and regional news matter, especially to older and housebound people.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: The unions representing people who make BBC programmes are calling for action on cuts, secure long-term funding, separate and secure funding for the World Service, and a formal voice for workers on a BBC board that remains independent in its editorial decisions.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: Cuts to staff and to the programmes the BBC pays others to make could reduce their quality and range, as well as threaten jobs and freelance work around the UK. MPs could question the Government about these choices before the next charter takes effect.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: I’m asking for a 90-minute debate before Christmas. A debate in the main Commons chamber would be our first choice.

turns.speaker: Will Stone
turns.text: A debate in the chamber needs at least 15 MPs to support the application. Could you find four more names, or would you accept a debate in Westminster Hall?

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: The most important thing is to have the debate before Christmas. I’m confident we can find more supporters: MPs from different parties have expressed interest, and Jo Stevens has said she supports it even though she hasn’t signed.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: A Commons committee has also reported on renewing the BBC charter, though only one member of that committee has signed this application. If a chamber slot isn’t available, we’d accept a 90-minute Westminster Hall debate.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: I sit on the Commons committee that looks at culture and media. I support the application. One example of the cuts is the planned end of You and Yours, the only live programme made for BBC Radio 4 outside London. Many of my constituents value its consumer coverage.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The committee staff will contact you. If the debate is on a Tuesday morning, it has to be on a morning when the responsible Government department is scheduled to reply.

turns.speaker: Grahame Morris
turns.text: I understand.

chapters.title: The next autism strategy
chapters.takeaway: Alison Hume argues that MPs should influence the replacement autism strategy while it is being prepared, given the severe inequalities autistic people face.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Alison Hume is asking for a debate in Westminster Hall on the Government’s priorities for its next national autism strategy.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: Autistic people still face some of society’s most serious health inequalities. They die between 6 and 15 years earlier than the general population. Only 26% of autistic students say they’re happy at school, and only three in ten autistic adults are in work.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: The Autism Act 2009 requires the Government to produce and regularly update a national strategy. But the House of Lords found that outcomes haven’t improved despite previous efforts.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: The current strategy expired at the end of June 2026. The Government says it remains committed to a new one and will extend the current strategy while it prepares the replacement.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: This is a timely chance for MPs from all parties to discuss the new strategy while it’s being developed, particularly as the Government introduces a new offer of support for children with special educational needs and disabilities. My application has cross-party backing.

turns.speaker: Mr Lee Dillon
turns.text: Those figures are alarming. Do you want the debate to coincide with a particular date, or would you accept the next available slot?

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: I’d be very happy with the next available slot.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Health Department would reply, and you’ve requested a Thursday, so the Tuesday scheduling restriction doesn’t apply. The committee staff will be in touch.
